title: Developer Experience Docs: Operating Procedures, Guides, and Canonical Fixes
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This page defines the operating procedures, standards, and canonical content for Developer Experience (DevEx) documentation at Redwood Inference. It covers the five core doc families we maintain: SDK guides, quickstarts and templates, API examples, docs-site operating procedures, and the canonical top support issues with reproducible fixes. The goal is consistent, high-quality documentation that reduces support load, accelerates developer time-to-value, and keeps public examples production-safe.

Audience

- Primary: Developer experience engineers, technical writers, solutions engineers.
- Secondary: SDK owners, product engineers, support engineers, developer advocates.

Scope

This page applies to all new and updated content under the eng-developer-experience space, including pages in: sdk-guides, quickstarts-and-templates, api-examples, docs-site, and support-top-issues. It does not replace handbooks for company-wide HR policies or legal content.

Ownership and Roles

- DevEx Docs Owner: eng-developer-experience team (primary contact: Aisha Patel).
- Reviewers: at least one SDK owner and one support engineer per doc type.
- Publishing: Docs merged to main/docs-site branch and deployed by devex-ci pipeline.

Doc Families and Standards

1) SDK Guides
- Purpose: Reference and migration guides for each SDK (Python, JavaScript, Go, Java).
- Structure: Short intro, quickstart snippet, API reference link, authentication, configuration, examples (sync/async), error handling, migration notes, and troubleshooting.
- Required sections for every SDK page: "Installation", "Authentication", "Quickstart", "Common Patterns", "Error handling & retries", "Performance tips", "Link to API examples".
- Code style: Follow the language-specific style guide stored in /confluence/eng-developer-experience/sdk-guides/style-guide. Use idiomatic constructs, avoid pseudo-code. Provide both sync and streaming examples where applicable.

2) Quickstarts and Templates
- Purpose: Minimal, runnable examples that onboard developers in <10 minutes.
- One canonical quickstart per product surface: text generation, chat, embeddings, reranking.
- Template repository mapping: each quickstart must reference a templates repo and include: README, minimal config (env example), docker-compose demo (optional), and CI smoke test (GitHub Actions snippet).
- Quickstart checklist: clear prerequisites, copy-paste commands, expected output sample, cleanup instructions.

3) API Examples
- Purpose: Answer the question "How do I call the API for X?" with concrete examples for REST and each SDK.
- Examples must be small (6–30 lines) and include: endpoint, full JSON payload, expected success and error responses. Where applicable, include streaming and function calling examples.
- Security: Never include customer keys or secrets. Use placeholder values and call out recommended secrets storage (e.g., env vars, vault).

4) Docs Site Operating Procedures
- CI/CD: All doc changes must go through pull requests targeting main/docs-site. The devex-ci pipeline runs linters, link-checker, code-snippet test runner, and staging deploy.
- Release cadence: Major doc releases synchronized with product releases. Minor updates can be published continuously.
- Versioning: Use semantic versioning for SDK docs and the docs site. Each SDK page header must include supported SDK versions and compatibility matrix for API surfaces.
- Build & deploy: 
  1. Open PR with doc changes.
  2. Assign required reviewers (1 SDK owner + 1 support).
  3. Address linter/linker failures.
  4. Merge to main/docs-site. Pipeline deploys to staging at /staging/docs; QA validates; merge to main triggers production deploy.
- Rollback: Revert the merge commit and re-run the pipeline. For urgent rollbacks, contact #devex-ops and notify stakeholders.

5) Top Support Issues and Canonical Fixes
- Purpose: Capture the most frequent support tickets and provide reproducible, minimal fixes that support and SEs can copy-paste. Update quarterly.
- Format per issue: title, symptoms, root cause, reproducible steps, fix (commands or code), post-checks, P0 mitigation if applicable.

Canonical Issues (examples)
- 1) Authentication Errors: "401 Unauthorized" when calling the API from a container
- Symptoms: Calls succeed locally, fail in container with 401.
- Root cause: Missing env var or environment variable not injected into container runtime; token mis-formatting (extra quotes).
- Repro steps: Start minimal container image and curl endpoint with env var absent.
- Fix: Ensure env var passed via docker run -e REDWOOD_API_KEY and verify with docker exec sh -c 'echo "${REDWOOD_API_KEY}"'. If quoting was added in CI secrets, strip quotes in the runtime: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=$(echo "${REDWOOD_API_KEY}" | sed 's/"//g').
- Post-check: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H 'Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY' https://api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/health returns 200.

- 2) Streaming Response Truncation in Node SDK
- Symptoms: Client stops receiving tokens after ~512 tokens for long responses.
- Root cause: Default chunk buffer size in upstream HTTP client and missing keep-alive header on proxy.
- Fix: Upgrade SDK HTTP client to >=1.4.2 and enable streaming keepalive in proxy config (nginx: proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection "keep-alive"). Add retry-open-stream logic per SDK streaming guide.
- Post-check: Run the streaming smoke test in /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/streaming-tests and confirm tokens >2048 received.

- 3) High Token Cost from Repeated System Prompts
- Symptoms: Unexpectedly high per-request token counts and cost.
- Root cause: Using a full system prompt on every call instead of reusing cached KV/prefix.
- Fix: Use reusable context via session tokens or prefix caching: include only delta messages in live requests and keep system prompt in pinned context (see caching patterns in docs). Add batching where possible.

Doc Authoring and Review Workflow (detailed)

1) Create new page from template: Use the "devex-doc" template in quickstarts-and-templates. Populate metadata fields at top of page body.
2) Write clear, reproducible examples. Run all code snippets locally and in CI snippet runner.
3) Create PR in docs repo and add the reviewers list. Add a JIRA ticket if the change is tied to a product release.
4) Reviewers must verify: accuracy, security (no secrets), readability, and link validity.
5) Merge after approvals and fix CI issues.
6) Tag release notes if change impacts public docs.

Quality and Observability

- Metrics to track: broken-link rate, time-to-first-merge, doc-pr-cycle-time, number of support tickets referencing docs.
- Quarterly review: owner performs a content audit (accuracy, API drift, performance tips) and updates quickstarts and top-issues list.

Templates and Boilerplate (where to find)

- devex-doc (page template) — minimal required headings and metadata.
- quickstart-template — README, env.example, smoke-test.yml.
- api-example-snippet-template — JSON payload + expected responses.

Appendix: Example Quickstart (Python text generation)

1. Prereqs: Python 3.11+, pip, REDWOOD_API_KEY set.
2. Install: pip install redwood-sdk==1.3.0
3. Quick example:
   from redwood import RedwoodClient
   client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY'])
   resp = client.generate_text(model='redwood-1.0', prompt='Write a short haiku about latency')
   print(resp.text)

Expected output sample: a 3-line haiku.

Cleanup: unset REDWOOD_API_KEY or remove test keys from secrets manager.

Contact and escalation

- For doc build failures: #devex-ci and eng-developer-experience on Slack.
- For urgent security or content issues: ping Aisha Patel and the security on-call.
